messages.content:
Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 69
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: Middle Eastern
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Fast Food Worker
  trauma_type: Stalking
  pcl5: 76

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Threat: Waking Alert: I wake during the night to check whether I am safe, Threat in Faces: I study people's faces and body language to detect if they are a threat, Door and Lock Checking: I repeatedly check that doors and windows are locked
  Memory: Olfactory Recall: When I think about the frightening event I can sometimes smell things that I smelt when the frightening event happened., Emotionless Recall: Sometimes I can recall what happened but feel completely numb, as if it happened to a stranger, Story Feels Unreal: The memory is so extreme it is hard to believe it actually happened to me
  Negative Appraisals: Thought Avoidance: If I think about the event, I will not be able to handle it, Identity Loss: I feel like I don't know myself anymore, Mistrust: People can't be trusted

Vignette:
Samira Haddad is a 69-year-old married Middle Eastern American woman who works the front counter and early prep shift at a fast food restaurant. When she describes the event that changed her life, she does so in a way that still sounds disbelieving, as though she is recounting something that happened to someone else. For months, a man began appearing wherever she was. At first he stood too long near the restaurant entrance during her shift, watching her through the glass while she wiped trays or filled coffee. Then she started seeing him near the bus stop after work, and once across the street from her apartment building at dusk. He did not need to say much to make himself terrifying. What stayed with Samira was the fixed attention, the waiting, the sense that he knew her routines. She remembers one evening fumbling with her keys at her building door, aware of him lingering behind her on the sidewalk, and the sharp smell in the air from grease clinging to her work clothes mixed with cigarette smoke from nearby tenants. Even now, when she thinks about that period, she can suddenly smell those same odors so vividly that it feels as if she is back at the entrance again.

In the weeks that followed, Samira never felt she could relax. She had come to believe that safety depended on vigilance. At night she began waking abruptly and sitting upright before she was fully conscious, listening for sounds in the hallway or outside the windows. She would get out of bed and check the front door lock, then the window latches, then return a few minutes later to make sure she had really checked them properly. Her husband would tell her the apartment was secure, but reassurance did not settle her for long. She felt she had to see it herself. During the day, she found herself studying people’s faces with unusual intensity, scanning expressions, posture, and the way someone held themselves, trying to decide who might turn dangerous without warning. At work this was especially exhausting. A customer lingering too long at the counter, a man who kept looking toward the kitchen, a stranger standing outside the restaurant window could pull her attention away from the order screen entirely. She would search their face first and hear their words second.

When she tries to talk about the stalking, Samira’s memory shifts in ways that unsettle her. Sometimes she can describe concrete details—the building doorway, the bus stop, the feeling of keys pressed into her palm—but she does so in a flat, distant tone, feeling almost nothing, “like it happened to another woman,” as she puts it. At other times the whole story feels so extreme that she struggles to believe it truly happened to her at all. She knows it did, yet the memory can seem unreal, too strange to fit with the life she thought she had. That unsettled quality has made her wary of thinking about it directly. She has come to believe that if she lets herself dwell on the event, she will not be able to handle what comes up. So she cuts off the thoughts when they begin, turns on the television, starts cleaning, or finds some other task to do with her hands.

Over time, this changed how she understood herself. Before, she thought of herself as practical, sociable, and strong, someone who had worked hard all her life and could manage whatever came. Now she says she does not know herself anymore. She feels older in a way that is not about age. The world seems reorganized around danger and doubt. She has become convinced that people cannot be trusted, especially strangers, though the suspicion easily spreads further than she wants it to. She notices herself scrutinizing coworkers as closely as customers, wondering about motives, watching for inconsistencies in tone or glance. This has narrowed her world. She keeps interactions brief, stays close to familiar routines, and hurries home after shifts rather than lingering or chatting.

Samira sought help only after her husband told her he could see how little she was sleeping and how tense she had become even inside their own home. She was embarrassed to come, worried that speaking about the stalking might make everything more vivid, but also tired of living as if she must stay on guard every hour. What frightens her most is the sense that she has lost the person she used to be and that if she allows the memories in, they will overwhelm her completely. What she hopes, quietly, is not to erase what happened, but to feel believable to herself again and safe enough to stop checking the locks in the middle of the night.
